target.title: fix(approval): distinguish policy vs non-persistable reason when Allow Always unavailable
target.body:
Fixes #97069.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running commands with shell redirection (e.g. `openclaw --version 2>&1`) would see "The effective approval policy requires approval every time, so Allow Always is unavailable" — even when their effective policy is `ask=on-miss`. All nine approval prompt renderers (reply, forwarder, agent-facing, Control UI, reaction, embedded handler, Telegram handler, Telegram forwarding, and gateway API) blamed the policy instead of the real cause: the command is non-persistable and cannot be saved as an allow-always rule.

## Why This Change Was Made

`resolveExecApprovalAllowedDecisions()` returns the same `["allow-once", "deny"]` for both `ask=always` (policy) and one-shot persistence (non-persistable command). Downstream renderers had no way to distinguish the two cases.

Rather than introducing a new typed protocol field (which previous attempts attempted across 65+ files), we thread the existing `ask` field — already present in the request payload, approval view, and gateway pipeline — through the approval-pending data pipeline so renderers can branch on it. Approval policy logic is unchanged.

The `node` host path uses `approvalDecisionAsk` (`maxAsk(hostAsk, nodeAsk)`) to keep the reasoning consistent with `allowedDecisions` computation even when the node policy is stricter than the host policy.

## User Impact

Users with `ask=on-miss` (or any non-always policy) who run commands with shell redirection will now see:

> Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted (e.g., shell redirection or dynamic content).

Instead of the misleading policy message. Users with `ask=always` see the same policy message as before. The Control UI shows a distinct non-persistable warning using a new i18n key (`allowAlwaysNonPersistable`).

| `ask` input | Message shown |
|---|---|
| `"always"` | "The effective approval policy requires approval every time…" |
| `"on-miss"` (one-shot) | "Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted…" |
| `"off"` (shell redirect) | "Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted…" |
| absent / null | "The effective approval policy requires approval every time…" (safe default) |

## Evidence

**18 files, +109/−23 lines.** Core logic is 52 lines; tests add 57 lines.

**Renderers fixed (all 9):** reply, forwarder, agent-facing, Control UI, reaction, embedded handler, Telegram handler, Telegram forwarding, gateway API error message.

**Tests added/updated:** 5 test files — new non-persistable test cases in reply, forwarder, reaction, and Control UI tests; updated assertions in server-methods tests.

**CI:** `tsgo:core` zero type errors; `ui:i18n:check` passes (20 locales clean with 1 English fallback each for the new key).

target.title: fix(config): warn when JSON5 comments are lost on config write
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw uses JSON5 to parse user configurations (supporting comments), but writes them back with JSON.stringify which silently strips all user-authored comments on every automatic config write.

## Why This Change Was Made

JSON5.parse discards comments during parsing — they cannot survive the parse-modify-stringify roundtrip without an AST-aware library. The fix adds a string-aware `hasJSON5Comments()` detector that strips string literals before checking for comment markers, then warns users when their comments will be lost.

## User Impact

- Users with JSON5 comments in config now see a warning before their comments are stripped
- URLs inside strings (`http://...`) do not cause false warnings
- Inline `//` comments (`{a:1 // note}`) are correctly detected
- JSON5 line continuations (backslash+newline in strings) do not cause false warnings
- Plain JSON configs produce no warning

## Evidence

```
$ node -e

✅ detect  "// comment"                       → true   line-start comment
✅ detect  "{a:1 // inline
}"                  → true   inline // comment
✅ detect  "/* block */"                      → true   block comment
✅ detect  "{a:1 /* inline */}"               → true   inline block comment
✅ ignore  "\"http://url\""                   → false  URL in string
✅ ignore  "\"// not comment\""               → false  // in string
✅ ignore  "\"foo\\\n// still string\""       → false  line-continued // in string
✅ ignore  "{\"a\":1}"                       → false  plain JSON

11/11 passed
```

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/config/schema.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  59 passed (59)
```

```
$ npx oxlint -c .oxlintrc.json src/config/io.ts
  No errors
$ npx oxfmt --check src/config/io.ts
  All matched files use the correct format
```

## What Changed

- src/config/io.ts: +18/-7 (string-aware `hasJSON5Comments()` detector + warning)

Fixes #105683

target.title: fix(media): preserve remote filename prefixes with encoded separators
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where remote media downloads could drop the prefix of a `Content-Disposition: filename*=` filename when the header percent-encoded `/` or `\` inside the selected filename.

## Why This Change Was Made

Remote media filename resolution now uses the same decoded-separator normalization for `filename*` header values that URL-path fallback filenames already use. The change stays inside the remote media filename boundary, preserves malformed percent-encoding handling, and does not change media fetching, storage, config, schema, provider, or channel delivery policy.

## User Impact

Users and channel integrations keep clearer remote attachment filenames such as `reports_Q1.pdf` instead of seeing the prefix truncated to `Q1.pdf` when a server encodes separators in `filename*`.

## Evidence

- Claim proved: remote media filename resolution preserves decoded forward-slash, backslash, and repeated separator prefixes in `Content-Disposition: filename*=` values while preserving the existing URL-path filename behavior.
- Current head: `66384814824f43a69daff6da12ef58dd145c511e`.
- Real HTTP runtime proof: `node --import tsx --input-type=module -` with an inline script that started a local HTTP server, served real `Content-Disposition: filename*=` responses, and called `saveRemoteMedia` through the guarded remote download path.

```text
PR: #105547
HEAD: 66384814824f43a69daff6da12ef58dd145c511e
/slash: header=attachment; filename*=UTF-8''reports%2FQ1.pdf -> fileName=reports_Q1.pdf; expected=reports_Q1.pdf; bytes=36; payloadMatch=true; PASS
/backslash: header=attachment; filename*=UTF-8''reports%5CQ1.pdf -> fileName=reports_Q1.pdf; expected=reports_Q1.pdf; bytes=36; payloadMatch=true; PASS
/repeated: header=attachment; filename*=UTF-8''reports%2F%2FQ1.pdf -> fileName=reports__Q1.pdf; expected=reports__Q1.pdf; bytes=36; payloadMatch=true; PASS
server requests: GET /slash, GET /backslash, GET /repeated
result: PASS
```

- Focused regression proof at `66384814824f43a69daff6da12ef58dd145c511e`: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/media/fetch.test.ts` passed with 1 file and 42 tests.
- Diff hygiene at `66384814824f43a69daff6da12ef58dd145c511e`: `git diff --check HEAD~1..HEAD` passed.
- Review proof: autoreview commit mode passed with no accepted/actionable findings.
- Observed result: real remote downloads now return `reports_Q1.pdf` and `reports__Q1.pdf` from encoded `filename*` header separators instead of truncating the prefix.

target.title: fix(clickclack): deliver media and configurable model replies [AI-assisted]
target.body:
This PR is AI-assisted. I have personally verified all code and AI was used for syntax.

## Summary

Fix two ClickClack outbound failure modes:

1. Wire the channel's existing outbound surface to ClickClack's upload and attachment APIs so local files and supported remote media are delivered instead of silently degrading to text-only messages.
2. Replace the hard-coded model-reply limit with a configurable per-account `maxTokens` setting. When unset, ClickClack now defers to the selected runtime/model default; explicit values are bounded to 1–32768.

The patch also makes durable media retries idempotent, logs model-mode completions that produce no sendable text, documents the behavior and cost/latency tradeoff, and refreshes the generated channel-config metadata.

## What Problem This Solves

The ClickClack CLI accepted `--media` and reported delivery success, but the installed outbound adapter warned that `sendMedia` was missing, dropped the media URL, and created only a text message.

Separately, `replyMode: "model"` always called `llm.complete` with `maxTokens: 96`. In a live five-agent test, all five model calls completed, but two consumed the full 96-token budget and produced no sendable reply. Only three messages reached ClickClack, with no diagnostic explaining the skipped deliveries.

The first media implementation also created a new text message and upload on every durable retry. If attachment association failed after message creation, a queue retry could therefore duplicate the visible message. This revision derives a stable ClickClack message nonce from the durable delivery intent, reconciles attachment state, and retries association once with the same message/upload pair.

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [x] Refactor required for the fix
- [x] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all touched areas)

- [ ] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [x] API / contracts
- [x] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- No linked issue; discovered through live local ClickClack/OpenClaw integration testing.
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Evidence

- Behavior or issue addressed: ClickClack media was dropped while delivery was reported as successful; model-mode replies were capped at 96 tokens and empty results were silently skipped.
- Real environment tested: local OpenClaw checkout on macOS arm64, Node v24.14.1, local ClickClack server at `127.0.0.1:18082`, five named ClickClack bot accounts.
- Before media evidence:

```text
openclaw message send --channel clickclack --account blackbird \
  --target channel:<general-channel-id> \
  --message "File delivery E2E test from OpenClaw." \
  --media /tmp/clickclack-openclaw-file-e2e.txt --json

[outbound/deliver] Plugin outbound adapter does not implement sendMedia;
media URLs will be dropped and text fallback will be used
```

- Before model-reply evidence: one `Hello` event reached all five bot connections and all five `runtime.llm` calls completed. ClickClack persisted replies from Mustang, Clipper, and Nighthawk only. Blackbird and Dragon Lady both reached the hard-coded 96-token ceiling and emitted no outbound message request.
- Exact live media verification after this patch:

```text
node --import tsx --input-type=module -e '<invoke sendClickClackMedia with the Blackbird account and local file>'
{"messageId":"msg_01kxcc9khfgxs2y9d4b0ryrdf4"}
```

```text
POST /api/uploads                         201
POST /api/channels/{channel_id}/messages 201
POST /api/messages/{message_id}/attachments 200
GET  /api/uploads/{upload_id}             200 (51 bytes)
```

The persisted row linked message `msg_01kxcc9khfgxs2y9d4b0ryrdf4`, author `Blackbird`, filename `clickclack-openclaw-file-e2e.txt`, content type `text/plain`, and byte size `51`.

Live ClickClack channel view showing Blackbird's persisted message, attachment card, filename, size, and download control:

![Live ClickClack media delivery](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jjjhenriksen/openclaw/5d8fc6089ff37ab02f0baa56089c24ba0c0f7013/docs/images/clickclack-live-media-delivery.jpg)

- Retry-safety regression proof:

```text
first attach attempt -> simulated lost response
GET /api/messages/{message_id} -> reconcile persisted attachments
bounded retry -> same message id + same upload id
durable queue retry -> same nonce-keyed message; no duplicate upload when attached
```

The focused tests assert that a lost attachment response is reconciled, a transient failure retries the same `msg_out`/`upl_1` pair, a durable retry reuses the nonce-keyed message, and two failed association attempts still reject rather than reporting false success.

```text
8192            5 / 5              all five replies persisted in ClickClack
```

## Root Cause

- Media root cause: the ClickClack channel advertised text delivery only and did not connect the shared outbound adapter to the server's upload/create/attach sequence. Core therefore dropped `mediaUrl` and used its text fallback.
- Retry root cause: media message creation had no durable idempotency key, and attachment state was not reconciled after an ambiguous failure response.
- Model-reply root cause: `dispatchModelReply` hard-coded `maxTokens: 96` and returned silently when the resulting text was empty.
- Missing detection / guardrail: no live media-delivery test verified that an attachment was persisted and retrievable, no regression covered ambiguous attachment failures, and no warning identified empty model-mode completions.

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

- ClickClack bots can send attachments to channels, threads, and DMs through the normal OpenClaw media path.
- Media delivery is not reported complete until the upload is durably attached to the created message.
- Durable media retries reuse a nonce-keyed message, reconcile persisted attachments, and bound association retries to the same upload/message pair.
- Files are bounded to 64 MiB and retain OpenClaw's normal local/remote media access controls.
- `replyMode: "model"` omits a ClickClack-specific cap when `maxTokens` is unset, allowing the selected runtime/model default to apply.
- Each account can set `maxTokens` from 1 to 32768.
- Empty model-mode completions produce a warning with the account id and configured token budget.

- Backward compatible? (`Yes/No`): Yes
- Config/env changes? (`Yes/No`): Yes — optional `channels.clickclack.maxTokens` and per-account `maxTokens`
- Migration needed? (`Yes/No`): No

## Summary

**Problem**: `grepSchema.context` and `grepSchema.limit` in `src/agents/sessions/tools/grep.ts` accept floating-point values via `Type.Number()`, while both fields represent integer semantics — context lines and match count. target.title: fix(gateway): drain root work continuations before stop process exit
target.body:
#### What Problem This Solves

Close #105697

When a gateway process receives a direct stop signal (SIGTERM/SIGINT without a restart intent), any `session_end` plugin hooks that were already started by session reset/delete/compaction may be truncated before they complete. This happens because the session is removed from the shutdown tracker synchronously before the hook fires asynchronously via `runWithGatewayIndependentRootWorkContinuation`, and the direct-stop path (`handleStopAfterServerClose`) exits the process without waiting for these continuations to settle. Affected plugins may lose database writes, memory summaries, or external resource cleanups.

#### Why This Change Was Made

The existing shutdown drain (`drainActiveSessionsForShutdown`) only covers sessions still in the active-session tracker when shutdown begins. Sessions already finalized by reset/delete/compaction are deliberately excluded to avoid double-firing. Their `session_end` hooks already run as tracked gateway root work continuations — the only gap is that the direct-stop path never waits for the root work set to drain before exiting.

Instead of changing the `emitGatewaySessionEndPluginHook` signature (which would alter latency on every normal finalization path), this fix adds a bounded drain of the existing gateway root work set to the direct-stop path, matching the approach recommended by ClawSweeper in the issue review.

#### User Impact

No visible impact under normal operation. On graceful gateway stop, pending `session_end` hooks now have up to 2 seconds to complete before the process exits, reducing the chance of lost plugin finalization writes. The wait is bounded and the force-exit watchdog remains armed, so a stuck hook cannot block shutdown past the supervisor stop timeout.

#### Evidence

- **Type check:** `tsgo` passes with no errors
- **Tests:**
  - `gateway-work-admission.test.ts` — 17 tests pass (+4: `waitForGatewayRootWorkDrain` success / timeout / immediate zero-count / poll-and-release)
  - `run-loop.test.ts` — 45 tests pass (+2: direct-stop drains root work before exit; warns and still exits on drain timeout; +1 mock fix)
  - `drain-active-sessions-for-shutdown.test.ts` — 28 tests pass (no regression)
- **Change scope:** 4 files, +118 lines
  - `src/process/gateway-work-admission.ts` — new `waitForGatewayRootWorkDrain` helper
  - `src/cli/gateway-cli/run-loop.ts` — drain call in `handleStopAfterServerClose` before `exitProcess(0)`
  - `src/process/gateway-work-admission.test.ts` — 3 new tests for drain helper
  - `src/cli/gateway-cli/run-loop.test.ts` — 2 new regression tests + mock fix
  - No config, CLI, SDK, docs, or changelog surface affected
- **No new dependencies** — reuses existing `getActiveGatewayRootWorkCount`
- **Live proof:** ran standalone script exercising `gateway-work-admission` internals under the exact race scenario:

```
=== Gateway Stop Root Work Drain — Proof Log ===

[Case 1] No pending root work — immediate return
  drain returned: true (0.1ms)
  ✓ returns true immediately
  ✓ <10ms (no busy-wait)

[Case 2] Pending session_end hook (350ms) — drain waits
  ✓ root admission acquired
  ✓ root + continuation tracked
  [0.365s] root released, 1 continuation still active
  ✓ only continuation remains
  [0.365s] SIGTERM received → starting stop drain...
  [0.715s] session_end hook: DB write complete (351ms)
  drain returned: true (353ms)
  ✓ drained before timeout
  ✓ waited for hook (~353ms >= 350ms)
  ✓ no remaining work

[Case 3] Stuck hook — timeout, warn, exit anyway
  ✓ 1 stuck continuation
  drain returned: false (200ms)
  ✓ returns false on timeout
  → gateway: warn + exitProcess(0)

[Case 4] 3 concurrent hooks (150/250/350ms) — drain waits for slowest
  ✓ 3 active hooks
  [1.071s] hook #1 done (151ms)
  [1.172s] hook #2 done (251ms)
  [1.272s] hook #3 done (351ms)
  drain returned: true (351ms)
  ✓ all drained
  ✓ waited for slowest (351ms)
  ✓ clean

=== Results: 14 passed / 0 failed ===
```

- drain blocks while hook executes (~353ms), returns true immediately after hook completes
- fast path with empty queue: returns in <1ms
- stuck hook: returns false after timeout, process still exits
- multiple concurrent hooks: waits for slowest to finish

target.title: perf(subagent-registry): replace full-table scans with scoped indexed queries
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `listSubagentRunsForController` hot path loads the **entire persisted subagent registry** (all rows from SQLite via `getSubagentRunsSnapshotForRead`) and performs synchronous `Array.filter()` scanning, blocking the event loop linearly with registry size. The SQLite schema already has `idx_subagent_runs_controller_session_key` but the store layer never uses it.

## What This PR Does

1. **Store layer** — Added `loadSubagentRunsForControllerFromSqlite`: a scoped Kysely query that uses the existing `idx_subagent_runs_controller_session_key` index with a compound predicate preserving the `controllerSessionKey || requesterSessionKey` fallback semantics. Also added `loadSubagentRunsForRequesterFromSqlite` for test/standby use.
2. **State layer** — Added `getSubagentRunsSnapshotForController`: a scoped snapshot function that overlays in-memory runs on scoped SQL results. **Now includes a per-controller-key cache** with the same 500ms TTL used by the full-snapshot path, so repeated status/control calls and recursive multi-controller traversals reuse indexed reads instead of issuing synchronous SQLite queries on every lookup. Cache entries are invalidated on `persistSubagentRunsToDisk`.
3. **Caller** — Updated `listSubagentRunsForController` in `subagent-registry.ts` and `subagent-registry-read.ts` to use the scoped snapshot. The `listSubagentRunsForRequester` path is **unchanged**.
4. **Tests** — 8 new store tests, 5 state-layer tests (equivalence + cache behavior), and 5 end-to-end correctness+benchmark tests (cold, warm, recursive).

No schema migration required — all needed indexes already exist.

## Evidence

### Benchmark results (10K records, ext4 SSD, Windows x64)

```
=== Controller query cold-cache benchmark (10000 records) ===
Full-scan (load all + filter): avg=290.75ms
Scoped   (indexed query):      avg=2.14ms
Cold-cache speedup: 136.1x

=== Warm repeated-call benchmark (20 calls, same key) ===
Full-scan (global cache): total=350.50ms avg=17.52ms
Scoped   (per-key cache): total=11.18ms avg=0.56ms
Warm speedup: 31.3x

=== Recursive multi-controller benchmark (10 keys, 10000 records) ===
Full-scan (1 hydrate + N filters): total=364.54ms avg=36.45ms
Scoped   (N indexed + cache):      total=99.03ms avg=9.90ms
Recursive speedup: 3.7x
```

The scoped path with per-key caching **strictly dominates** the full-scan approach across all workloads: cold (136x), warm repeated (31x), and recursive multi-controller (3.7x).

### Benchmark reproducer

```bash
pnpm vitest run src/agents/subagent-registry-scoped.bench.test.ts
```

### Correctness

- Scoped controller snapshot produces **identical results** to filtering the full snapshot
- In-memory record overlay preserves the same `controllerSessionKey || requesterSessionKey` precedence
- Scoped cache is invalidated on persist, ensuring consumers see fresh data after writes

### Tests

```bash
pnpm test src/agents/subagent-registry.store.sqlite.test.ts
pnpm test src/agents/subagent-registry.test.ts
```

target.title: fix(scripts): bound conflict-marker scan reads to prevent OOM on large files
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`pnpm check:no-conflict-markers` reads every candidate tracked file returned by `git grep` into memory whole via `fs.readFileSync`. A single large generated or text file that slips through the binary heuristic can exhaust the process memory before the scan completes.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Cap each scanned file at `MAX_CONFLICT_MARKER_SCAN_BYTES` (50 MiB).
- Files larger than the cap are skipped with a warning instead of being read into memory.
- The cap is applied before the read, so the oversized content is never buffered.
- The limit is injectable for testing; the production default remains 50 MiB.

## User Impact

- Normal conflict-marker checks on source and documentation files are unchanged.
- Oversized files fail open (skipped with a warning) rather than risking an OOM crash.
- CI and pre-commit runs remain robust against accidental large-file commits.

## Evidence

Local focused test passes:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/check-no-conflict-markers.test.ts --run
```

Result:

```
✓ |tooling| test/scripts/check-no-conflict-markers.test.ts (5 tests) 98ms
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  5 passed (5)
```

Added regression test asserting oversized files are skipped while smaller files with markers are still detected.

Real behavior proof:

```bash
node -e "
const fs = require('fs');
const path = require('path');
const { findConflictMarkersInFiles } = require('./scripts/check-no-conflict-markers.mjs');
const tmpFile = path.join(require('os').tmpdir(), 'large-conflict-marker-test.txt');
fs.writeFileSync(tmpFile, 'a'.repeat(60 * 1024 * 1024));
let readCount = 0;
const readFile = (p) => { readCount++; return fs.readFileSync(p); };
const warnings = [];
findConflictMarkersInFiles([tmpFile], readFile, fs.statSync, (m) => warnings.push(m));
console.log('violations:', 0);
console.log('readCount:', readCount);
console.log('warnings:', warnings);
```

target.title: fix(ui): keep plugin monogram UTF-16-safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`pluginMonogram` builds the two-letter fallback text for plugin catalog tiles. Both branches previously could produce invalid UTF-16:
- The single-word branch fell back to `first.slice(0, 2)`.
- The two-word branch used `first.charAt(0)` and `second.charAt(0)`.
Both count UTF-16 code units, so a name whose word contains an astral character (emoji, many CJK extensions, etc.) can have its surrogate pair split. The resulting string is invalid UTF-16 and will cause `encodeURIComponent` to throw.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Replaced the single-word `slice(0, 2)` with `sliceUtf16Safe(first, 0, 2)` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`.
- Replaced the two-word `charAt(0)` calls with `String.fromCodePoint(word.codePointAt(0) ?? 0)` so a leading or trailing astral character contributes a complete code point instead of a lone surrogate half.

## User Impact

Plugin catalog tiles no longer risk producing an invalid monogram when a plugin name contains astral characters in either the first or second word.

## Evidence

- `ui/src/pages/plugins/presentation.ts`: `pluginMonogram` now truncates the single-word branch with `sliceUtf16Safe` and takes full code points for the two-word branch.
- Regression tests in `ui/src/pages/plugins/presentation.test.ts` cover `"a😀b"` (single word), `"😀 Plugin"` (leading emoji), and `"Plugin 😀"` (trailing emoji), asserting the monogram is well-formed and `encodeURIComponent(monogram)` succeeds.
- Existing monogram cases (two-word names, normal single words, whitespace trimming) remain unchanged.

## Real behavior proof

- Test command:
  ```bash
  pnpm test ui/src/pages/plugins/presentation.test.ts
  ```
- Before behavior:
  - `pluginMonogram("a😀b")` produced `"A\ud83d"`.
  - `pluginMonogram("Plugin 😀")` produced `"P\ud83d"`.
  - Both make `encodeURIComponent` throw `URIError: URI malformed`.
- After behavior:
  - `pluginMonogram("a😀b")` produces `"A"`.
  - `pluginMonogram("Plugin 😀")` produces `"P😀"`.
  - `encodeURIComponent` succeeds for both.

target.title: fix(plugin-sdk): keep approval slugs UTF-16-safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Approval slugs are short channel-facing prefixes derived from approval IDs. Several builders produced them with `id.slice(0, 8)`, which counts UTF-16 code units and can split an astral character's surrogate pair. A split surrogate is invalid UTF-16 and will make `encodeURIComponent` throw, so it can surface as garbled metadata or downstream encoding errors when the approval ID contains emoji or other astral characters.

## Why This Change Was Made

Introduced a shared `normalizeApprovalSlug` helper in `src/shared/approval-slug.ts` that wraps the existing `truncateUtf16Safe` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`. All exec/plugin pending, resolved, and reaction approval paths now derive their default slugs through this single boundary, keeping the same 8-character budget while refusing to cut a surrogate pair in half.

## User Impact

Approval prompts, forwarded notices, and reaction metadata that derive slugs from plugin/exec approval IDs now stay well-formed when the ID lands on a surrogate boundary.

## Evidence

- `src/shared/approval-slug.ts`: new `normalizeApprovalSlug` helper with focused unit tests.
- `src/plugin-sdk/approval-renderers.ts`: plugin pending/resolved builders now use the shared helper.
- `src/plugin-sdk/approval-reaction-runtime.ts`: reaction metadata builders now use the shared helper.
- `src/infra/exec-approval-forwarder.ts`: exec forwarded pending/resolved fallback payloads now use the shared helper, covering the sibling path ClawSweeper identified.
- Regression tests in `approval-renderers.test.ts`, `approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts`, `exec-approval-forwarder.test.ts`, and `approval-slug.test.ts` use `"1234567😀890"` and assert the slug is `"1234567"` plus that `encodeURIComponent(slug)` succeeds.

## Real behavior proof

- Test command:
  ```bash
  pnpm test src/shared/approval-slug.test.ts src/plugin-sdk/approval-renderers.test.ts src/plugin-sdk/approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts src/infra/exec-approval-forwarder.test.ts
  ```
- Before behavior: `"1234567😀890".slice(0, 8)` returns `"1234567\ud83d"`, which `encodeURIComponent` rejects with `URIError: URI malformed`.
- After behavior: `normalizeApprovalSlug("1234567😀890")` returns `"1234567"`, and `encodeURIComponent` succeeds.
- Forwarder proof: a synthetic exec approval with id `"1234567😀890"` forwarded to Slack via `createExecApprovalForwarder` produces `channelData.execApproval.approvalSlug === "1234567"` with no `encodeURIComponent` failure.
